qs.q: Which ABO group is the universal plasma donor?
qs.explain: Group AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B, so it is the universal plasma donor. Group O is the universal RED CELL donor; the plasma and red cell rules run in opposite directions.

qs.q: A patient's plasma agglutinates both reagent A1 and B cells. What is the group?
qs.explain: Reverse typing reads antibodies: agglutinating both A1 and B cells means anti-A and anti-B are present, group O. No agglutination of either cell is group AB.

qs.q: Which test asks whether red cells are already coated with antibody inside the body?
qs.explain: The direct antiglobulin test uses the patient's washed red cells (in vivo attachment). The indirect test, which includes the antibody screen, looks for free antibody in plasma.

qs.q: Which transfusion reaction allows the same unit to be restarted?
choices: Allergic, skin only and fully resolved
qs.explain: Only the allergic reaction confined to the skin that completely resolves after a pause and an antihistamine may restart the SAME unit, more slowly, within the 4-hour hang time. Fever, wheezing or hypotension: never restart.

qs.q: Which finding separates anaphylaxis from an acute hemolytic reaction?
qs.explain: Anaphylaxis has NO fever; the acute hemolytic reaction brings high fever with rigors. Both can cause shock and dyspnea and both start during the transfusion.
